SGOV and BIL returned about 3% this year, beating the Nasdaq, S&P 500 and Dow even after counting stock dividends.

Including dividends, QQQ is down about 1% and DIA is up about 1%, so both trail bill funds.

The Fed raised rates in September, and a quarter-point December hike is seen as close to certain, which should lift bill payouts.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

Jeffrey Gundlach, chief executive of DoubleLine Capital, posted on X at 11:58 a.m. ET on Friday as stocks slipped: "YTD the NASDAQ has underperformed T-Bills." At 12:41 p.m., he followed up: "YTD the DJIA and the S&P 500 have underperformed T-Bills."

luchschenF / Shutterstock.com

He posted no figures, so we ran them ourselves. We used the iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (NYSEARCA:SGOV) and the SPDR Bloomberg 1-3 Month T-Bill ETF (NYSEARCA:BIL) as proxies for a T-bill holder, and as of the November 20 close, the numbers support him on all three indexes.

On Friday, the S&P 500 fell 3.70% for its seventh straight loss and finished the week down 8.4%, and the NASDAQ Composite dropped 5.28% on the day.

A sharp rebound could reverse this within days. If you're determining how much to hold in cash, the result still shows what 2026 has paid for so far, and it shows the rate outlook going into the Fed's December meeting.

Stocks Trail Cash Even on Price Alone

The S&P 500 closed Friday at 6,910.39, compared with 6,845.50 at the end of 2025. That works out to a 0.95% gain.

The Dow closed at 48,147.33, compared with 48,063.29 at year-end, for a gain of just 0.17%. The NASDAQ Composite finished at 22,617.73, below its 23,241.99 starting point, and is down 2.69% for the year.

The Nasdaq-100 closed at 25,028.98 on Friday, November 20, 2026, after a 5.61% drop that erased 1,488.07 points. That close left the index 49.41 points above the bear market line.

Courtesy of POOLCORP

Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) fell 5.67% to $608.45 on volume of 134.5 million shares, nearly double Thursday's. Heavy volume on a down day indicates that selling was broad.

The record close came on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, only about six weeks earlier. The index is now down 0.87% for 2026, and Friday's close was its lowest since April 8, 2026.

As of Friday's close, the Nasdaq-100 remains outside bear market territory. A drop of about 0.2% on Monday, November 23 would change that, so QQQ owners need to decide whether the label matters.

How Thin the Margin Is

A bear market is commonly defined as a close at least 20% below the record close. The Nasdaq-100's record close of 31,224.47 sets that line at 24,979.58.

Friday's close was 19.84% below the record, but the session low of 24,910.48 was 20.2% below it. Some outlets measure from the intraday record of 31,361.37, which raises the line slightly.

Friday was the worst session since November 5, when the index fell 6.36% and lost 1,807 points, its largest one-day point loss. The 10.43% weekly drop was the worst since the week ended March 20, 2020.

title: Wall Street’s Fear Index Just Hit 9.7. History Says the S&P 500 Could Rally 10.5% in 3 Weeks
detail:
Wall Street’s Fear Index Just Hit 9.7. History Says the S&P 500 Could Rally 10.5% in 3 Weeks
Rich Duprey

SPY dropped 9% this week and QQQ lost 16% in a month, pushing fear to its first sub-10 reading since March 2026.

After sub-10 fear readings since 2021, the S&P 500 gained an average of 9% over three weeks, the sturdier guide.

Morgan Stanley argued the S&P 500 is poised to jump, while Goldman Sachs released a 2027 outlook calling for gains.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

Friday's session produced the kind of reading that usually shows up near market lows. CNN's Fear & Greed Index fell to 9.7 on Friday, November 20, according to The Kobeissi Letter. That is its fourth-lowest reading since the 2022 bear market and its first below 10 since March 2026. The gauge dropped 30.6 points, or 76%, in six trading sessions, its fastest slide since February 2025.

Mario Tama / Getty Images

Real losses drove the panic. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) fell 3.55% Friday, 8.56% for the week and 10.77% over the past month. Tech took the worst of it. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) lost 5.67% Friday and 16.1% in a month. Coverage this week has faulted the damage on an AI sell-off.

Stocks Have Historically Rebounded After Sub-10 Readings

The last three times the index fell below 10, the S&P 500 gained an average of 10.5% over the following three weeks. Across every sub-10 reading since 2021, the average three-week gain was 9%. When nearly everyone who wanted to sell has already sold, it takes very little buying to lift prices.

Don't read too much into the 10.5% figure, though. It averages just three events, so one strong rebound can skew it. The 9% figure covers more readings and is the better guide. Both still point the same way: extreme fear has tended to come near the end of a selloff.

------

------

Options Traders Are Paying Up for Protection

The options market backs up the fear reading. The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) closed at 28.44 on November 19, up 52.1% in a week. That close ranks in the 99.2 percentile of the past 180 days. The full-chain put/call ratio on SPY options stands at 1.48, which means investors are buying more downside protection than upside exposure.

Even so, the VIX has stayed below 30, the level that usually marks a full-blown panic. Fear is high but has not yet turned into surrender.

Falling Bond Yields Are a Quiet Tailwind

The bond market is cushioning the blow. The 10-year Treasury yield slid to 4.92% on November 20, down from 5.15% a week earlier. Lower long-term rates make stock valuations easier to justify and bring down mortgage costs. Strategists are also angling bullish: Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) argued this week that the S&P 500 is poised to jump, and Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) released a 2027 outlook calling for gains.

What This Means for Your 401(k)

The longer-term damage is smaller. Even after the past month, SPY is still up 1.16% year to date and 5.71% over 12 months. Households, though, were gloomy well before stocks fell. University of Michigan consumer sentiment was 48.0 in October, below the 60 level that has historically lined up with recessions. A stock rebound can happen quickly. Repairing household confidence takes longer.

For long-term savers, past sub-10 readings have historically been followed by rebounds within weeks. The bigger risk sits with anyone drawing down a portfolio right now, since an early-retirement drawdown does far more lasting damage than the same drop fifteen years in (we mapped that sequence-of-returns problem, and how to defend against it, in a free guide here).

Signals to Watch Before Mid-December

VIX above 30: A close there would mean fear is still building and hasn't topped out.

10-year yield below 5%: If yields climb back above it, the valuation support from lower rates goes away.

Nasdaq 100 stability: This selloff began in tech, so a rebound in QQQ needs to lead any recovery.

If all three hold, the historical three-week rally pattern has a real chance of playing out again. If the VIX breaks above 30, a 9.7 reading may mark the middle of the selloff, with the lows still ahead.

title: She Moves $250,000 of Her 401(k) Into a Nasdaq-100 Fund at 60 to Own Anthropic From Its Debut Thursday. Nasdaq’s Fast-Entry Rule Keeps Her Fund From Buying Until Dec. 21, After Any First-Month Pop
detail:

Quick Read

Nasdaq's fast-entry rule keeps Anthropic out of QQQ and similar funds until Dec. 21, so her $250,000 misses any first-month pop.

Anthropic would likely make up about 3% of the index, roughly $7,500 of her money, so her fund is mostly a concentrated AI-hardware bet led by NVDA.

Trades inside a 401(k) avoid capital gains tax, but withdrawals count as ordinary income that can raise Social Security taxes and Medicare premiums; Roth conversions before 63 sidestep the premium hit.

The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

A 60-year-old with about $1 million in her 401(k) moved $250,000 into a Nasdaq-100 index fund through her plan's brokerage window this week. She wanted to own Anthropic from its first trade on Thursday. The move cost her nothing in taxes, but her fund won't hold a single Anthropic share until Dec. 21.

Morsa Images / Getty Images
Why Her Fund Can't Buy Anthropic Until Dec. 21

Nasdaq adopted a fast entry rule in March, having taken effect in May. It lets large IPOs into the Nasdaq-100 after just 15 trading days, so they no longer have to wait for the annual December reconstitution.

Anthropic's trading began Thursday, Nov. 19, which puts day 15 on Dec. 10. StockAnalysis, citing Bloomberg, put the timing plainly: "Anthropic is on track to join the Nasdaq 100 on December 21, so index funds will have to buy its shares."

Until that date, Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) and similar trackers hold no Anthropic. Any first-month pop happens without her. On Dec. 21, every Nasdaq-100 fund buys at the same time, at whatever price the market sets that day. S&P 500 funds face a longer wait, because S&P declined to fast-track new listings. Those IPOs must wait 12 months and become profitable first.

------

Now Available: The 401k Answers Nobody Gives You.

For many Americans, funding a 401(k) only leads to more retirement questions. Should you roll your 401k into an IRA, and when? What's the tax impact if the rollover check gets made out to the wrong name? When do required withdrawals begin, and how much do you have to take?

Fisher Investments put the answers in one place. 401k & IRA Tips and Answers is free, and it covers rollovers, contribution limits, required withdrawals, and what actually belongs inside the account once the balance gets serious. Read More Here ›

------

Napkin Math: $250,000 Buys a Slice of Anthropic

The IPO range was $70 to $78, which values Anthropic at about $1.4 trillion at the top.

For scale, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) is worth about $3.5 trillion and makes up about 8% of QQQ.

If you scale that weight down to Anthropic's size, it lands near 3% of the index. At best, that's roughly $7,500 of her $250,000, and Nasdaq's float cap could shrink it further. Treat this as a rough estimate. The real weight depends on Nasdaq's methodology and on Anthropic's price on Dec. 21.

She already owns more of the Anthropic story through NVIDIA, with about $20,000 of her position in that one stock. NVIDIA's expanded partnership gives Anthropic access to Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin capacity. On its latest call, NVIDIA said Anthropic's annualized revenue hit $81 billion at the end of October. It also expects frontier labs to supply approximately 15% of its data center revenue.

Owning Anthropic through NVIDIA also means owning NVIDIA's problems. Shares are about $146, down 33% in a month, after the company's longtime chief executive resigned. Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. Earnings held up: Q3 non-GAAP EPS was $2.68 against a $2.47 consensus.

NVDA Price Scenario — 24/7 Wall St.

Beyond Nvidia, QQQ's next-largest holdings include Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) at 7% and Micron (NASDAQ:MU) at about 5%. In practice, her $250,000 is a concentrated position in AI hardware held five years before Medicare.

Tax-Free Trade Today, Ordinary Income Later

Trading inside a traditional 401(k) triggers no capital gains tax. When she takes the money out, though, it is taxed under section 72 as ordinary income (26 U.S.C. § 402(a)). If the AI trade works, every dollar of gain eventually reaches her tax return at ordinary rates.

Those withdrawals can set off a chain of other costs. Under 26 U.S.C. § 86(a)(2), up to 85% of Social Security benefits can become taxable once income passes the thresholds.

Medicare adds a second layer. For a single filer above $109,000, the Part B premium rises from $203 to $284 a month. Add the Part D surcharge and that first tier alone costs about $1,148 a year.

Medicare uses a two-year lookback, so the premium she pays at 65 is set by her tax return from age 63. A big withdrawal at 63 to lock in AI gains could raise her taxes that year and her Medicare premiums two years later.

Timing works in her favor. Because she was born in 1966, her RMDs don't start until age 75, with the first one due for 2041. That leaves her early 60s open for planned withdrawals and Roth conversions.

Three Moves Before Dec. 21

Trade size follows from the goal. If owning Anthropic is the point, $250,000 of Nasdaq-100 exposure buys only a small slice of it. The choice is between the whole index and just the IPO, and the trade size follows from that choice.

Total NVIDIA exposure is often larger than it looks. Most large-cap index funds already hold NVIDIA, so the top-10 holdings across every fund in a portfolio add up to what functions as one stock position.

Roth conversions before age 63 stay off her Medicare bill. Income between the ages of 60 and 62 will not raise her premiums because she's not enrolled in the program yet. Starting at age 63, modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) gets counted toward future premiums, which is where the IRMAA surcharge tier comes in. In 2026 the first tier starts at $109,000 for single filers. Later, qualified charitable distributions of up to $111,000 a year (the 2026 limit) can offset RMDs.

Key Points

Interested in Schwab US Dividend Equity ETF? Here are five stocks we like better.

Dividend-focused ETFs have held up better than the broader market during the recent sell-off, offering investors a way to maintain equity exposure.

SCHD and LVHI offer lower volatility and dividend income, although LVHI carries higher expenses.

VYM provides broad diversification and low fees, but its substantial Broadcom holding leaves some exposure to the technology sector.

Over the past month, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA: SPY) has fallen nearly 5%, while the tech-heavy Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ) has dropped about 8%, as the sell-off in AI and semiconductor stocks spilled over into the broader market.

For more conservative investors, the instinct in moments like this can be to step aside entirely. But exiting the market altogether risks missing the rebound when sentiment eventually turns. A middle ground might be to rotate a portion of capital into funds built to absorb less market turbulence, staying invested while dialing down overall volatility.

→ Greg Abel Makes His Next Moves: Inside Berkshire's Q3 Portfolio

With the 10-year Treasury yield sitting just above 5%, investors purely chasing income can currently earn more, with less credit risk, in government bonds than in any of the funds below. So the case for these three ETFs is stability first, with stock market exposure maintained and dividends serving as a supporting benefit rather than the main attraction.

Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF: Quality Screens and a Defensive Tilt

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSEARCA: SCHD) tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which filters companies on measures such as cash flow, return on equity, and dividend growth history.

→ Grounded at 52-Week Lows: When Will Boeing Stock Take Flight?

The result is a portfolio of about 100 mature, cash-generative businesses, with names such as Procter & Gamble (NYSE: PG), Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO), and Chevron (NYSE: CVX) among its largest positions.

That makeup has translated into steadier price action. SCHD carries a beta of 0.68 and has held roughly flat over the past month, even as the S&P 500 slid.

It remains up more than 26% year to date and sits less than 5% below its 52-week high.

At just 0.06% in annual expenses, it is one of the cheapest funds in its category and yields about 3%.

Its top 10 holdings, however, make up roughly 41% of assets, so it is more concentrated than its holding count might suggest.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Stocks had three strong years. VOO, the Vanguard S&P 500 fund, returned 26.3%, 25.0% and 17.8% in 2023, 2024 and 2025, with dividends reinvested. Then stocks turned. VOO lost 5.3% in November through the Nov 19 close. It ended Thursday, Nov 19, 8.1% below its Oct 6 record.

Here is the answer for a $1 million mix of 60% stocks and 40% bonds that nobody touched. Started three years ago in VOO and BND, the Vanguard bond fund, it is now 68.7% stocks. Started five years ago, it is 71.4% stocks. The owner chose 60%. The market chose the rest.

The usual advice in a fall is to stay calm and stay diversified. This article looks at something quieter. It looks at drift, the way a mix moves away from its target as one part grows faster.

How far has the untouched mix drifted?

The three-year portfolio is worth $1,440,185 at Thursday's close. Getting it back to 60/40 means moving $125,754 from VOO to BND. The five-year portfolio would need $156,326 moved.

The drift was larger at the top. On Oct 6, when VOO set its record, the five-year portfolio was 73.4% stocks. Since then it has lost 5.5%. A portfolio reset to 60/40 that day lost 4.2%. On this portfolio, that reset would have saved $19,022.

The five-year VOO and BND mix went into this fall 73.4% in stocks, not the 60% its owner picked. If that money is your retirement savings, every extra point in stocks is more of the drop you have to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018, and it pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's. See how it held up.

Did bonds cushion this month's fall?

Not in November. BND slipped 0.55% in November through Thursday, so bonds fell with stocks this month.

Bonds did help when measured from the top. Since the Oct 6 stock record, BND has gained 1.6%. VOO fell 2.0% on Thursday alone. BND rose 0.06% the same day.

What did resetting at past tops save?

We checked every S&P 500 fall of 20% or more since Dec 1998. For each one, we took a $1 million 60/40 set three years before the top and never re-balanced. We compared it with the same money reset to 60/40 on the day of the top. No one can pick that day in advance, so these savings show what a perfectly timed reset did.
